A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GMN-based NeRF representation-learning work despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 and the appendices report original latent-space analyses, classification experiments, and instance-level and class-level retrieval results.

after.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original classification, retrieval, and loss-comparison results, including hash-based NeRF experiments and ObjaNeRF retrieval examples.

M1.justification: Section 3 adds a parameter-graph conversion for multi-resolution hash tables using table-entry and feature nodes. Training changes from fixed MLP/tri-plane pairs to randomly selected pairs among three architectural families. The GMN encoder, nf2vec decoder, and underlying rendering and SigLIP loss forms remain.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates ShapeNetRender objects represented by MLPs and tri-planes. v2 adds hash-based NeRF inputs and ObjaNeRF/Objaverse queries against ShapeNetRender galleries, introducing a distinct data distribution and retrieval scenario. The separate quantitative class-level retrieval evaluation in v1 Appendix A is removed.

E2.justification: nf2vec and Cardace et al. remain the evaluated external comparators in corresponding single-architecture classification experiments: v1 Tables 2/4 and v2 Tables 3/5. No new external baseline is evaluated. The contrastive-only variant remains evaluated in v2 Appendix C.

E3.justification: Multi-architecture training changes from BOTH to ALL, with three representations per object and revised pair sampling. v2 adds hash depth, width, level-count, and table-size test configurations, plus cross-dataset retrieval with no matching instance in the gallery. Class-recall evaluation disappears. Appendix B retains the original ShapeNet splits, training epochs, batch sizes, and optimizer settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds hash-level/table-size sensitivity tests and cross-dataset retrieval robustness cases, including the LR versus LR+C ObjaNeRF comparison in Figure 9. The three-loss latent-space analysis is revised for three families. The separate seen-versus-unseen MLP t-SNE analysis in v1 Figure 5 and Appendix C is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both present point estimates and qualitative visualizations.

E6.justification: Multi-architecture results are replaced under changed training conditions. For example, MLP-to-TRI LR+C recall@1 is 41.2% with BOTH training in v1 Table 5 and 30.6% with ALL training in v2 Table 10; these do not establish a controlled performance decline. Retrieval favors LC in v1 and LR+C in v2. Single-architecture MLP/TRI results remain unchanged, hash results are added, and class-level retrieval scores disappear.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix A adds a mathematical graph-size comparison: the hash representation requires N(T+F) nodes and NTF edges, versus O(N(R^3+F)) nodes and O(NR^3F) edges for explicitly represented voxel grids. This supplies a new complexity argument absent from v1, without adding a broader theorem or proof framework.

C1.justification: v2 adds first-time weight-space processing of hash-based NeRFs as a central contribution. Its introduction and conclusion qualify unseen-architecture generalization to variants within training families, replacing v1's broader arbitrary-architecture language. Single-architecture performance claims also shift from matching or exceeding prior methods to superiority/state-of-the-art performance.

C2.justification: v1 presents LC as preferable for strong architectural invariance; v2 favors LR+C because LC weakens class separation. New interpretations discuss hash-table subclusters, sensitivity to table size, and Objaverse retrieval failures. The stated main limitation changes from missing hash-based validation to training and quantitative evaluation concentrated on ShapeNetRender.

D1.justification: Appendices A/B/D add exact graph attributes, hash hyperparameters, and NerfAcc implementation information. Reported hardware changes from RTX 3090 to RTX A6000. Core encoder/decoder and training hyperparameters, training-time estimates, and the planned code release remain. Conversely, v1's explicit cosine retrieval distance and NeRF input frequency-encoding widths are no longer specified.

R1.justification: The existing GMN, nf2vec, and contrastive-learning positioning remains. v2 adds focused references on hash-based NeRFs, ObjaNeRF/Objaverse, and NerfAcc, and explicitly distinguishes its hash-table graph construction from the constructions borrowed from Lim et al. This extends the retained research positioning rather than replacing it.

P1.justification: Beyond the title change, v2 substantially reorganizes the exposition: existing MLP/tri-plane graph descriptions move to Appendix A, Section 3's loss motivation is condensed, architecture descriptions are consolidated, and LC results receive a dedicated Appendix C. The introduction, conclusion, and qualitative-analysis narrative are substantially rewritten.

P2.justification: The main text switches from two columns to one. Figures 1–2 incorporate hash inputs; architecture Tables 1/7 and detailed graph Figure 5 are added. Result tables gain reorganized rows/columns and family-based highlighting, while retrieval montages are redesigned and expanded. The class-retrieval table and unseen-MLP t-SNE display are removed.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's stated main limitation—untested hash-table NeRFs—with a concrete graph construction, complexity justification, and substantial classification, retrieval, and architectural-variation evidence. It also better qualifies the scope of generalization. These gains materially strengthen the central contribution despite removing class-level retrieval scores, the unseen-MLP visualization, and some reproducibility details. Objaverse evidence remains qualitative, and changed training conditions prevent interpreting revised scores as controlled performance gains.
